issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Daniel, a 38-year-old European American teacher, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on edge following a mugging that had taken place one night while he was walking from his car toward his apartment. He had been close enough to the building to think he was home, carrying his bag and keys, when two men approached him suddenly in the dark. The details of the robbery remained sharply fixed in his mind: the fast movement up beside him, the shouted demand, the pressure of fear before he could even make sense of what was happening. One of the men shoved him and took his wallet and phone, and Daniel remembered the whole episode not as a story he chose to tell, but as something that could seize him without warning. When the memory returned, it did not arrive as a distant recollection. He described it as coming back all at once, so that he could taste what he had tasted during the event, and the scene would feel completely real across his senses, as though he were back on that street with the same darkness, the same proximity of bodies, and the same helplessness pressing in from every direction.

In the months afterward, Daniel found that the memory would force its way into his mind when he least wanted it to. It would interrupt ordinary moments, sometimes in the middle of preparing for work or sitting with his wife at home, and once it came back so fully while he was teaching that he had to pause at the front of the classroom to steady himself. He did not describe a single image so much as an overwhelming return of the whole event, vivid in a way that made him feel exposed and physically present in it. Since the robbery, he had become alert to signs of danger in almost every environment. He studied people's faces and body language whenever he was around strangers, looking for the slightest indication that someone might pose a threat. Entering a room or building, he immediately scanned for exits without thinking about it, as if orienting himself to where he could go if something went wrong. Unexpected movement nearby would make him react as though he were in danger, even when the movement was harmless, and he noticed how quickly his body would tense before he had time to decide what was happening.

Several situations had become especially difficult for him. Crowded places were increasingly hard to tolerate, particularly when people were close enough that he could not easily track everyone around him. He found himself less willing to go into busy stores or public events, and the discomfort had begun to shape how he and his wife spent their weekends. Driving with other people also became upsetting for him, especially when someone else was in the car and he felt unable to manage the surroundings himself. Loud noises were another clear trigger; a sudden bang, a shouted voice, or a sharp sound could make him jump and leave him feeling shaken for a long time afterward. These reactions were not abstract to Daniel. They showed up in the daily routines of his life, including the crowded hallways and busy staff areas of the school where he worked. He became more guarded in the building, more attentive to who was approaching him and how quickly, and he noticed himself choosing routes and exits with unusual care.

As time passed, Daniel came to believe that what happened to him had been deeply unfair and that no one had done anything about it. He felt let down by the people and institutions that should have protected him, and that sense of disappointment sat beside a broader conviction that the world was a dangerous place. Even now, he spoke as someone who had once assumed that a walk home from work would be ordinary and safe, and who now moved through the same kinds of spaces with a different expectation. The mugging had not only left him distressed by the memory of what happened; it had changed the way he understood public spaces, strangers, and his own vulnerability in everyday life. He finally sought help after noticing how much effort it took to get through ordinary days without feeling constantly watchful, and how often the strain was spilling into his work and home life. What he most wanted was to feel safe enough to move through the world without always checking faces, exits, and sudden movements, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never again experience crowded streets or public places as anything other than places where danger might appear without warning.
